PRD Structure: Pricing the Claims a Document Makes

Most treatments of the product requirements document describe its sections. The more useful question, and the one experienced practitioners actually argue about, is a different one: which claims in a PRD are expensive to be wrong about, who can prove them wrong, and how soon. Answer that, and the structure follows. Answer it badly, and no template saves you.

The argument of this page: a PRD is not a description of a product. It is a ledger of falsifiable claims, each priced by the cost of being wrong about it, arranged so that every claim reaches the person who can falsify it soonest and most cheaply. Sections, length and template are downstream of that. Once you accept it, several long-running disputes — narrative versus specification, living versus frozen, prose versus executable spec — stop being matters of taste and become questions about the cost structure of a particular decision.

1. Two documents, two deadlines, February 2026

On 9 February 2026, Aditya Rao, VP of Product at Nirmiti Instruments in Pune, had thirty-one days before a printed-circuit-board revision froze. Nirmiti makes cold-chain instrumentation: a battery-powered logger the size of a matchbox that sits inside insulated shippers carrying vaccines and biologics, a cellular gateway that sits on the wall of a distribution warehouse, and a cloud service that turns the resulting temperature traces into the compliance record that a pharmaceutical distributor must be able to produce on demand. Roughly 41,000 loggers were in the field across seventeen distributors. The devices ran eighteen months on a single lithium thionyl chloride cell, carried 256 kilobytes of flash, and sampled every five minutes.

The feature Aditya had to specify was not exotic. Distributors wanted the system to warn them before a temperature excursion, not after: a shipper whose internal temperature was drifting toward the upper bound of the 2–8 °C range for refrigerated product would be flagged while the consignment could still be re-iced, rather than written off on arrival. The commercial case was straightforward — the seventeen distributors had between them written off product worth about ₹9.4 crore in the previous financial year to excursions discovered on delivery. The engineering case was not. Prediction implied a higher sampling rate, higher sampling implied battery draw, battery draw implied either a larger cell or a shorter service life, and the cell footprint was a mechanical decision on a board that was about to be committed to a contract manufacturer in Noida. A respin after the freeze cost Nirmiti ₹38 lakh in non-recurring engineering and tooling, and fourteen weeks.

Aditya therefore had a document to write in which one particular class of sentence — anything that implied a sampling interval, a cell chemistry or a board footprint — was, in practical terms, irreversible, while another class of sentence, about how the alert appeared in the distributor's dashboard, could be changed any Thursday afternoon. His problem was not how to write a PRD. It was how to write one document whose sentences had a spread of reversal costs across four orders of magnitude, and to keep the reader aware of which was which.

Eight hundred kilometres away, in Bengaluru, Rhea Sabharwal was writing a document with the opposite pathology. Rhea was Director of Product at Nirakaar Systems, which sold an AI agent to third-party administrators in health insurance. When a hospitalisation claim arrived incomplete — a missing discharge summary, an unreadable pharmacy bill, a prescription that did not name the treating doctor — Nirakaar's agent conducted the follow-up conversation with the claimant over WhatsApp: it asked for what was missing, read what came back, and judged whether the file was now sufficient to send to the adjudicator. A large TPA processing about 62,000 claims a month had put a pilot contract on the table with a signing date of 3 March 2026. First-pass document completeness across that TPA's book sat at 31 per cent. The pilot's threshold was 55 per cent.

Rhea's requirements were all reversible. The agent's behaviour lived in prompts, retrieval configuration and a small classifier; any of it could be changed and redeployed in under two hours at effectively zero marginal cost. And yet the document was harder to write than Aditya's, because almost nothing the agent did could be stated as a branch. "The agent must ask for the discharge summary when it is missing" is not a requirement; it is a hope, because whether the summary is missing is itself a judgement the agent makes about an image a claimant photographed at 11 p.m. in a hospital corridor. The system's deliverable was a distribution, not a behaviour. And the genuinely irreversible commitment in the room was not code at all. It was the sentence in the contract that said what the agent would never do — under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority's claim-handling expectations, an agent that told a claimant their file was complete when it was not would produce a rejection weeks later, at the worst possible moment in the customer's life, and the TPA's grievance ratio would carry it.

Two PMs, two PRDs, one shared difficulty: knowing which sentences in the document were load-bearing and which were decoration. Everything that follows is an attempt to make that judgement teachable.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Define the object precisely. A product requirements document is a written artefact that converts a validated problem into a set of claims a build team can act on without guessing, and a reviewer can contest without ambiguity: who the product serves, what problem is being solved and what is deliberately not, the intended shape of the solution, the behaviours the system must exhibit, and the measurements that will later settle whether it worked. Six moving parts — personas, problem, goals and non-goals, solution, requirements, metrics — in an order where each constrains the next. That skeleton is stable across four decades and almost every industry. What is not stable, and what the schools fight about, is how much of the document should be prescriptive, and at what level of abstraction it should stop.

The intellectual history matters here, because each school is a reaction to a failure of its predecessor. The oldest lineage is requirements engineering proper, formalised in United States defence practice (MIL-STD-490 and its descendants) and later in IEEE Std 830-1998 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148: a software requirements specification is a numbered, uniquely identifiable, individually testable list, and traceability from requirement to test to release is a first-class obligation. This tradition was built for systems where a defect is measured in lives or in hundreds of crores, and it has never been refuted; it has been outgrown by domains where it is disproportionate. Its intellectual high-water mark is arguably David Parnas and Paul Clements' 1986 essay A Rational Design Process: How and Why to Fake It, which conceded that no real team derives a system top-down from a complete specification, and then argued that teams should nonetheless produce the documentation such a process would have produced — because the document's value is as an artefact for the reader, not as a record of the writer's actual thinking. That is a subtle and still under-appreciated claim, and it is the direct ancestor of the position taken on this page.

Against that, the commercial software lineage: the market requirements document of the 1980s, written for sales, was reworked in Silicon Valley practice into a PRD written for engineers, and the canonical statements of PM responsibility from that period — Ben Horowitz's 1995 Netscape memo, Marty Cagan's later writing — treat the document as the thing that distinguishes a PM who defines a product from one who relays requests. The third school is the agile reaction of the 2000s: Kent Beck and Ron Jeffries' user story as card, conversation and confirmation, with the card explicitly a placeholder for a conversation rather than a specification, on the argument that written requirements decay faster than they can be maintained and that co-located teams should replace documents with dialogue. The fourth, the narrative school, is Amazon's working-backwards practice — a press release and FAQ written before the product exists, on the argument that prose forces the writer to confront gaps a bulleted list lets them skip. Basecamp's Shape Up pitches belong loosely here too, with an added and important move: fix the time budget, vary the scope, and deliberately specify at a coarse "fat marker" resolution so that the team retains the room to trade scope for schedule.

A fifth position has emerged recently and does not yet have a settled name: the executable-specification school, running from Gojko Adzic's specification-by-example and behaviour-driven development through to the current practice of writing a spec precise enough that a coding agent can implement it. Its claim is that prose requirements are a lossy intermediate representation and should be replaced, wherever possible, by artefacts that machines can check — scenarios, fixtures, evaluation sets.

The whole practical skill of PRD writing is knowing which regime a given sentence is in, and the uncomfortable fact is that in Aditya's document both regimes appear on the same page.

3. Mechanics: the claim ledger and what it costs to be wrong

Expert practitioners, whatever they say about templates, do something functionally identical: they read their own draft line by line and, for each assertion, answer three questions. What kind of claim is this? Who can prove it false? What does it cost if we find out late? The sections of the PRD are a convenient filing system for the answers, and their conventional order is not arbitrary — it runs from claims whose falsifier is a customer, through claims whose falsifier is a colleague, to claims whose falsifier is a machine.

Exhibit 2. The conventional section order is a cost ordering. Claims that can be cheaply falsified by a person are filed first; claims that can only be falsified by shipping are filed last. The practical implication is that a PRD is written badly whenever a cheaply-falsifiable claim is buried inside a section that nobody reads until week ten — the commonest instance being an assumption about a persona's workflow smuggled into a requirement line.

Two second-order effects fall straight out of this picture, and both are usually left implicit. The first is that a PRD's requirements section is an anchor. The moment engineering estimates against a document, the numbers in that document acquire a gravitational pull that no subsequent conversation fully escapes — teams revise estimates by adjusting from the anchor, not by re-deriving. That is a reason to be scrupulous about what appears as a number and what appears as a placeholder: an unbaked figure written as "≈90 seconds" in a draft will be built as ninety seconds. Expert writers mark uncertainty explicitly rather than relying on the reader to infer it, using a confidence marker per requirement — settled, provisional, open — and they treat any requirement still marked "open" at the spec review as a scheduling risk with a named owner and a date, not as a detail.

The second is that non-goals are negotiating capital, not documentation. A non-goal written down early is cheap to hold; the same refusal made in week seven, under pressure from a sales commitment, costs political capital the PM may not have. This is why experienced PMs write more non-goals than feel necessary, and why they distinguish carefully between a refusal ("we will not do this, on principle, and here is the principle"), a deferral ("not in this release, and here is the trigger that would change that"), and an exclusion ("this is someone else's document"). The three read alike and behave completely differently under pressure.

Pricing a sentence: the arithmetic Aditya ran

Aditya's team had a working heuristic, never written down until he wrote it into the PRD's front matter. For any claim in the document, the expected cost of leaving it ambiguous is the probability that two competent readers resolve it differently, multiplied by the cost of discovering the divergence at the stage where it would surface. Nirmiti's numbers: a loaded engineering day cost about ₹9,500. A specification review involving six people cost roughly ₹6,000 an hour of everyone's time. Discovering an ambiguity during the review was therefore a ₹6,000-scale event. Discovering the same ambiguity in integration testing, at around week nine, cost on Nirmiti's own retrospective data about seventeen engineer-days of rework across firmware and cloud — ₹1.6 lakh — plus roughly two weeks of schedule. Discovering it after the board froze cost ₹38 lakh and fourteen weeks.

Run that on a specific sentence. The draft read: "the device shall increase its sampling rate when a thermal drift is detected." Aditya judged the probability that his firmware lead and his cloud lead would resolve that differently at about 0.4 — the firmware lead would naturally read "device" as autonomous on-board logic, the cloud lead would read it as a command pushed down from the server, and the two readings imply completely different power budgets and completely different board decisions. The sentence sat squarely in the class whose error surfaces after the freeze. Expected cost of ambiguity: 0.4 × ₹38 lakh, or ₹15.2 lakh. Cost of a focused hour making it unambiguous: ₹6,000. The ratio is not close.

Formalise it slightly, because the formalism is what tells you when to stop. Suppose the probability of divergent reading falls roughly exponentially with the hours s spent specifying a claim: P(s) = P₀·e−s/τ, where τ is the number of hours it takes to cut the ambiguity by a factor of e — for a well-understood domain, two to four hours. Let C be the cost of late discovery and w the hourly cost of the people doing the specifying. The marginal hour is worth spending while (P₀/τ)·e−s/τ·C > w, which solves to an optimal depth of s* = τ·ln(P₀C / τw).

For Aditya's sampling sentence, with P₀ = 0.4, C = ₹38,00,000, τ = 3 hours and w = ₹6,000: s* = 3 × ln(15,20,000 / 18,000) = 3 × ln(84.4) ≈ 13.3 hours. Thirteen hours on one requirement sounds absurd until you notice that it is what the arithmetic says, and that Nirmiti had in fact spent three days the previous year recovering from exactly this ambiguity in a different feature. For Rhea's equivalent — the exact wording the agent uses when asking for a missing pharmacy bill — with C at perhaps ₹40,000 (a redeploy, some support noise, a day of someone's attention) and the same P₀, τ and w, the formula gives 3 × ln(16,000 / 18,000), which is negative. The correct specification depth is zero. Do not write it down; write the evaluation instead.

Exhibit 3. Marginal value of an additional hour of specification, (P₀/τ)·e−s/τ·C, against a flat marginal cost of review time. The hardware claim justifies roughly a day and a half of argument; the AI wording claim justifies none. The formula is crude — P₀ and τ are judgements, not measurements — but it is directionally right, it is auditable, and it makes explicit the thing that PRD templates hide: uniform depth across a document is almost always wrong.

The step that is always left implicit: classifying the state space

The mechanic that most reliably separates a strong requirements section from a weak one is not writing more requirements. It is enumerating the state space and then classifying every cell of it, including the cells where nothing special happens. Aditya's device had six operating states (normal logging, drift-suspected, excursion-active, low-battery, firmware-updating, factory-reset-pending), four connectivity states (gateway in range, out of range with buffer available, out of range with buffer full, roaming on a foreign network) and three alert states (none, sent-unacknowledged, acknowledged). That is 72 combinations. No sane PRD enumerates 72 behaviours.

What Aditya's PRD did instead — and what the exp20-level treatment of this topic does not reach — was classify all 72 into three buckets and account for every one. Eleven combinations received an explicit specified behaviour, because they were either dangerous or commercially significant: a drift-suspected device with a full buffer and no gateway in range, for instance, must prioritise retaining the drift samples over the routine five-minute samples, because the routine trace can be reconstructed by interpolation and the drift cannot. Forty-nine combinations were declared "behaves as normal logging" in a single sentence with a stated rationale. Twelve were flagged as open, each with a named owner and a date. The value of this is not completeness for its own sake; it is that the twelve open cells became visible as schedule risk in week one rather than as defects in week nine, and that the forty-nine explicitly dismissed cells prevented a well-meaning engineer from inventing behaviour for them.

4. When the idea applies, when it does not, and when it actively misleads

The conditions under which a full PRD earns its cost can be stated as four testable claims. Test them against both protagonists rather than nodding at them.

Three of four conditions hold for Nirakaar, which is why Rhea still wrote a PRD. But the fourth fails, and that failure is the whole design problem of her document. Where specifiability fails, a PRD that attempts to specify behaviour in prose is not merely wasteful — it is actively misleading, because it produces a document that looks authoritative and is not, and because the team will build to the prose and then discover that the prose never constrained the thing that mattered. The correct move, and the one Rhea made, was to keep the six sections but replace the requirements section's content with three different kinds of claim: invariants that must hold on every single interaction and can be enforced deterministically ("the agent never states that a claim will be approved"; "the agent never echoes a policy number back in full"), distributional targets stated with sample sizes and confidence intervals ("on the frozen evaluation set of 400 claims, the agent's judgement that a file is complete is correct at least 92 per cent of the time, measured against adjudicator ground truth"), and escalation rules that define what happens when the model's own confidence falls below a threshold.

There is a second misleading regime, less often discussed. When the problem itself is genuinely unknown — early discovery, a new market, a product where the team cannot yet name the persona without guessing — a PRD is worse than useless, because writing one forces premature commitment to a persona and a problem statement, and the document's authority then protects the guess from correction. The diagnostic is blunt: if you cannot write the problem section without the phrase "we believe", you are not ready to write a PRD; you are ready to write a solution hypothesis and a test for it. The third misleading regime is the very small and very reversible: a copy change, a pricing-page tweak, a configuration toggle. The PRD's overhead is fixed and its benefit scales with fan-out and reversal cost; below some threshold — most teams put it at about a week of one engineer's time on a fully reversible change — the document costs more than the errors it prevents.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The interesting failures happen where a document meets an organisational boundary, because a PRD's implicit assumption is that one author can hold one coherent intent, and organisations are built to violate that.

Hardware plus software. Nirmiti's case is the canonical one, and its defining feature is that different sections of the same document have different freeze dates. The mechanical claims freeze first, the firmware claims next, the cloud claims last, and the dashboard claims never really freeze at all. Mature hardware organisations handle this not by writing one PRD but by a layered structure: a product requirements document that states what the product must do for the customer, a hardware requirements specification derived from it that states the physical and electrical constraints, and a separate software PRD whose freeze date is months later. The layer that is almost always missing, and that Aditya insisted on, is an explicit derivation record — a short table showing which hardware constraint exists because of which customer-facing requirement. Without it, a later PM looking at a 90-second wake-up interval in the firmware spec has no way to know whether it is a physical necessity or a decision someone made on a Tuesday, and so treats every constraint as immovable.

Two-sided and marketplace products. A marketplace PRD must specify requirements for at least two populations whose interests are not aligned, and the structural trap is that the document is usually written by someone whose incentives sit on one side. The tell is a goals section with a demand-side metric and a non-goals section that is silent about supply. Practitioners who have been burned once write an explicit "effects on the other side" subsection with its own guardrail metric, and treat a change in the counterparty's economics as requiring that counterparty's representative to sign the document — which in an organisation with separate demand and supply PM teams means the PRD has two owners and a genuine negotiation, not one owner and a courtesy review.

Regulated products. In regulated domains the PRD stops being a purely internal artefact. For software regulated as a medical device, or for a lending product under Reserve Bank of India digital-lending expectations, or a claims process under IRDAI, a subset of the document's claims become evidence, and evidence has different properties from prose: it must be versioned, dated, attributable and immutable after the fact. The practical consequence is that mature regulated companies split the PRD in two — a working document that changes freely, and a controlled subset (usually the non-goals, the safety-relevant requirements and the traceability matrix) that moves only through a change-control process with signatures. Companies that do not split them end up either freezing a document that needed to keep moving or contaminating their audit trail, and both are expensive in different ways.

AI-native products. Rhea's difficulty generalises. When the system's output is a distribution, the PRD's centre of gravity shifts from the requirements section to two artefacts that classical PRD practice barely mentions: the evaluation set and the invariant list. The evaluation set — a frozen, versioned, representative collection of inputs with agreed ground truth — is the requirement, in the operational sense that it is what the build is checked against. The PRD's job becomes specifying the evaluation set rather than the behaviour: how many cases, sampled how, labelled by whom, with what inter-rater agreement, refreshed on what cadence. A PRD for an AI feature that does not say who labels the ground truth and how disagreements between labellers are resolved has left out its most load-bearing sentence.

Multi-product and platform seams. When a change crosses products, the honest unit is not one PRD but a contract. What mature organisations actually do — as against what their process documents say — is write a thin, stable, slow-moving document describing the interface and the invariants, owned by a single named person with authority to refuse changes, and then let each team write its own fast-moving local PRD against it. The failure mode of the alternative is described in section 8 below, and it is expensive.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. The requirements section is a negotiation with the future, and its tense matters.
A competent practitioner writes requirements in the present tense describing the system as built. An expert writes them as constraints on all acceptable implementations, which is a different sentence. "The dashboard shows unacknowledged alerts in red" describes one implementation; "an unacknowledged alert must be distinguishable from an acknowledged one at three metres, without colour being the only distinguishing channel" constrains the space and happens also to satisfy accessibility requirements nobody had raised. The tell in the wild: a requirements section that a designer reads and feels no room in. The obvious reading — that a more specific requirement is a better requirement — is wrong, because specificity spent on the implementation is specificity taken from the constraint, and the constraint is the part only the PM can supply.
2. The document's audience is not the team; it is the team plus the argument you will have in week seven.
Most of a PRD's value is realised in disputes, not in construction. Experts write with a particular future argument in mind and place the sentence that settles it where the arguer will find it. Rhea's PRD contained a paragraph explaining why the agent would not tell a claimant that their file was complete, only that nothing further was currently required — a distinction that sounds like pedantry until the week-seven conversation in which someone proposes friendlier wording. The tell: a PRD whose most-quoted sentences during the build are in the goals section, not the requirements section. That is a healthy document. The obvious reading — that the requirements section is the important part — is wrong; the requirements section is the largest part, which is not the same thing.
3. Baselines are a requirement, not a metric.
A target without a clean pre-change baseline is unfalsifiable, and an unfalsifiable metric is a decoration. But the deeper point is that capturing the baseline is often work — Rhea discovered that "first-pass completeness" had never been measured consistently across the TPA's three intake channels, and that establishing it required two weeks of instrumentation before a single line of agent code was written. Experts therefore write baseline capture into the requirements section as a deliverable with an owner, not into the metrics section as an assumption. The tell: a metrics section quoting a baseline to two decimal places that nobody can name the query for. The cost of catching this late is that you ship, and then cannot say whether it worked, which is indistinguishable from it not having worked.
4. Non-goals age differently from goals, and must carry an expiry condition.
A goal is satisfied and retires. A non-goal persists, and persists past the point where its original justification holds, until someone notices that the company has been refusing to build something for three years for a reason that expired eighteen months ago. Experts write each non-goal with the condition under which it should be revisited attached: "not until we have a signed data-processing agreement covering outpatient records", not merely "out of scope". The tell: a non-goal whose justification is a fact about the company rather than about the world. The obvious reading — that non-goals are about discipline — is half right; they are also about scheduling a future reconsideration.
5. The solution section should be short enough to be wrong.
A long solution section is a design document in disguise, and it has two costs: it invites the review to become a design critique, which consumes the reviewers' limited attention on the part of the document that is cheapest to change; and it makes the solution feel settled before the requirements have been stress-tested. Aditya's solution section ran to 280 words for a feature whose requirements section ran to nine pages. The tell: a spec review in which more than half the comments are about the solution section. The obvious reading — that a fuller solution description helps the team — is wrong in a specific way: it helps the team build faster and helps the reviewer catch less.
6. Depth should be allocated per claim, not per document.
This is the operational content of Exhibit 3, and it is the single most common thing competent practitioners get wrong, because templates enforce uniformity. A well-written PRD is visibly lumpy: two pages of painstaking argument about the one irreversible thing, and a single sentence for a whole area that is cheap to change. The tell: a document in which every requirement has roughly the same number of words. That is a document written to a template rather than to a risk profile, and it means the author has not distinguished the ₹38 lakh sentence from the ₹4,000 sentence.
7. Traceability is a chain of four, and it breaks at the third link.
Requirement → acceptance criterion → telemetry field → release criterion. Teams routinely establish the first link and the fourth, and skip the third: they define what "done" means and what "launch-worthy" means, and then discover after release that the system emits no event from which either can be computed. The expert habit is to write, next to each requirement that maps to a metric, the name of the event and the fields it must carry. The tell: a metrics section that names a rate but not a numerator event. The cost of catching this late is one release cycle of blindness, which in Rhea's case would have meant a pilot whose success criterion could not be evaluated within the pilot window.
8. "Living document" is a claim about a phase, not about the document.
A PRD should move freely until the estimate is made against it, and then move only through logged change, because an estimate is a function of a document and silently changing the input invalidates the output. Experts mark the transition explicitly — a dated line saying "estimated against revision 6" — and treat every subsequent change as requiring a re-estimate or an explicit acceptance that the estimate now excludes it. The tell: a team that cannot say which revision the schedule was based on. The obvious reading, that agility means the document should always be current, is wrong: it should always be current and always carry the record of what was promised against which version, which are different obligations.
9. The scarce resource has moved from writing to reading.
For forty years the binding constraint on specification depth was the cost of writing. Drafting a thorough PRD took days, and the discipline of PRD writing was largely a discipline of economy. That constraint has substantially dissolved: a competent PM with a language model can produce fifteen plausible pages in an afternoon. The constraint that has not moved is the cost of a senior engineer, a compliance reviewer and a designer reading fifteen pages carefully. The consequence is that the optimisation problem has inverted — the skill is no longer producing sufficient detail but routing it, so that each reviewer encounters exactly the claims they can falsify and none of the claims they cannot. The tell: a PRD that got longer this year without getting more decisions into it, and a review meeting where three people are silently skimming.

Stage changes the document's weight more than its shape, and the relationship is not linear in headcount — it is linear in the number of calendars that must be coordinated. A twelve-person company with one release train writes three-page PRDs because the fan-out is one; a hundred-person company with four release trains and a compliance function writes twelve-page PRDs not because it has grown fond of paperwork but because the same ambiguity now costs four times as many recoveries. The useful stage-specific observation is about the transition: the moment a company's PRDs should get materially heavier is not a headcount milestone but the first time a requirement must be agreed by two teams that cannot be put in the same room within twenty-four hours. Teams that make the change after that moment rather than before pay for it once, visibly, in a slipped integration.

One place where the difference is commonly asserted and is largely not real: the claim that consumer products need less rigorous requirements than enterprise ones. What consumer products need less of is permissioning and audit detail. The rigour required in the metrics section is if anything higher, because the feedback loop is statistical rather than conversational — an enterprise PM finds out from a customer call that the feature is wrong; a consumer PM finds out from a metric, and only if the metric was defined correctly beforehand.

8. Three worked examples

(a) Nirmiti: the requirement that saved a respin

The disambiguation exercise on the sampling sentence took Aditya eleven hours across three sessions, close to the thirteen the arithmetic predicted. The resolved requirement read: drift detection runs entirely on-device with no dependency on gateway connectivity; on drift detection the device raises sampling from one sample per 300 seconds to one per 60 seconds for a maximum of 45 minutes per event and a maximum of six events per 24 hours. The maxima were the part that mattered, and they came out of a power budget worked in the document itself. The logger's baseline draw at 300-second sampling was about 14 µA average; at 60-second sampling roughly 38 µA. Six events of 45 minutes is 4.5 hours a day at the elevated rate, or 18.75 per cent of the duty cycle, giving an average of 0.1875 × 38 + 0.8125 × 14 ≈ 18.5 µA. Against the 2,400 mAh cell, with a 0.85 usable-capacity derating for temperature and self-discharge, that is 2,040,000 µAh ÷ 18.5 µA ≈ 110,000 hours of theoretical life, comfortably past the 18-month (13,000-hour) warranty even after the substantial additional draw of the radio. Without the caps — that is, if drift detection could have triggered indefinitely on a badly insulated shipper sitting in a Nagpur transit yard in May — the same arithmetic ran the device to continuous 60-second sampling at 38 µA and pulled the margin down sharply once radio duty was included. The caps cost two lines in a PRD. Their absence would have been discovered as warranty returns at month fourteen across a field of 41,000 devices.

(b) Nirakaar: specifying a thing that cannot be specified

Rhea's requirements section contained twelve invariants and four distributional targets. The central target: on a frozen evaluation set of 400 historical claims, stratified to match the TPA's actual mix of 68 per cent cashless and 32 per cent reimbursement, the agent's "nothing further required" judgement must be correct in at least 92 per cent of cases, where correct means the adjudicator subsequently raised no further document query. The asymmetry mattered more than the headline number, and the PRD said so: a false "nothing further required" — telling a claimant they are done when they are not — was assigned roughly eight times the cost of a false "still missing", because the first produces a rejection three weeks later and a grievance, while the second produces mild annoyance and one more photograph. That 8:1 ratio was not a modelling detail hidden in a notebook; it was a product decision, stated in the PRD, from which the operating threshold was derived. At the chosen threshold the agent's recall on genuinely-complete files fell to 74 per cent, meaning a quarter of complete files got one unnecessary follow-up question. Rhea wrote that number into the goals section as an accepted cost, so that nobody would later treat it as a defect. Completeness on the pilot's first full month came in at 51 per cent against the 55 per cent threshold — short, but the shortfall was traceable to a stratum the evaluation set had under-sampled (claims from hospitals without digital discharge systems), which is the useful kind of failure: diagnosable, because the document had said how the sample was drawn.

(c) Nishtha Lending Cloud: the PRD written at the wrong altitude

The instructive failure belongs to a third company. Nishtha Lending Cloud, in Mumbai, operated a co-lending platform connecting three partner lenders to a network of originating agents. In 2025 it set out to unify borrower consent capture across all three partners — a genuinely valuable change, since inconsistent consent flows were the largest single source of file rejection. The PRD was, by any conventional standard, good: forty-seven numbered requirements, a clear problem statement, measured baselines, a thorough metrics section. It was also a single document covering work that crossed four engineering teams with four different release cadences, and it had a single author and no per-requirement owner.

The failure mechanism was not ambiguity in the usual sense. Each of the four teams read the document, understood it, and implemented it correctly within their own boundary. The divergences were at the seams: what "consent captured" meant at the moment of capture versus at the moment of persistence, whether a re-consent invalidated a prior consent's downstream artefacts, and which system was authoritative when two disagreed. None of those questions belonged inside any one team's requirements; all of them had been assumed away by a document that described the flow end-to-end as though one system executed it. Integration testing began in week eleven and did not converge. The programme slipped five months, cost approximately ₹2.1 crore in direct engineering time, and during the slip one partner lender withheld a volume increase representing about 38 per cent of planned incremental disbursal.

The recovery is the part worth studying, because it was structural rather than heroic. Nishtha split the single document into a thin contract PRD — eleven pages, owned by one principal engineer with explicit authority to refuse changes, containing only the interface, the state machine for a consent record, the invariants that must hold across all systems, and the versioning rules — plus four local PRDs, one per team, each written against the contract and each with its own owner and its own schedule. A second change mattered as much: an assumption register, in which any team could log an assumption it had made about another team's behaviour, with a named person on the other team required to confirm or deny it within three working days. In the first fortnight the register collected thirty-one assumptions, of which nine were false. Under the old structure, all nine would have surfaced in integration. The rebuilt programme shipped eleven weeks after the restart. The lesson Nishtha's VP of Engineering drew, and repeated afterwards, was that the document had not been insufficiently detailed — it had been detailed at the wrong altitude, describing an end-to-end experience when what four teams needed was a contract and four local specifications.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disputes are live, and it would be dishonest to resolve them here. Each is stated in the strongest form its proponents hold.

Should a PRD prescribe behaviour at all, or only outcomes? The outcome school — strongly associated with empowered-team practice — holds that a PM should specify the problem, the customer, the constraints and the measure of success, and stop; the team, which knows more about what is buildable, should determine behaviour. The evidence is real: teams given behaviour to implement consistently generate fewer alternatives than teams given a problem to solve, and the best solutions often come from an engineer who saw a cheaper path. The prescriptive school answers that this works only when the team is stable, senior, co-located in time zone if not in space, and operating on reversible software — and that in every other case "outcomes only" delegates not creativity but ambiguity, which the team resolves privately and inconsistently. What would have to be true for the outcome school to be wrong in a given case: that the cost of inconsistent private resolution exceeds the value of the alternatives forgone. Aditya's board freeze makes that true; Rhea's redeploy-in-two-hours makes it false. Both practitioners are right about their own case and would argue vigorously if put in a room.

Is the narrative or the structured document the better vehicle? The narrative school's evidence is that structured templates permit fluent nonsense — a well-filled template can be internally consistent and strategically incoherent, and prose exposes this because a reader notices when a sentence does not follow. The structured school's evidence is Nishtha: narrative describes experience, and experience is precisely the wrong unit when four systems must compose. The genuine synthesis nobody holds would be "write both", which most organisations lack the reviewer-attention budget for. What would falsify the narrative position: evidence that teams reading PR/FAQ-style documents make the same seam errors as teams reading structured ones, at similar rates. That study has not been done convincingly.

Should requirements be prose, or executable? The executable-specification position has strengthened considerably with AI builders: if a coding agent implements from the document, ambiguity is punished immediately and visibly, and the document acquires a fast feedback loop it never had. Its opponents make an argument that deserves more weight than it usually gets — that executable specifications are precise about the things that are easy to make executable, and silent about the things that are not, and that the silent things (why this matters, what we are deliberately not doing, what would change our mind) are where most product failures originate. The sharpest version of the objection: an executable spec cannot express a non-goal. What would have to be true for the executable school to win outright: that non-goals and rationale can be carried in a machine-checkable form without becoming so elaborate that nobody maintains them.

For AI features, is behavioural specification possible at all? One camp holds that an evaluation set simply is the specification, and that prose about how the model should behave is at best a summary of the eval and at worst a fiction. The other holds that an eval set specifies only what was sampled, generalises poorly to the tail, and cannot express invariants that must hold on inputs nobody thought to sample — which is precisely where the reputational and regulatory damage occurs. Rhea sits, uncomfortably, with a foot in each camp: her twelve invariants are prose, enforced by deterministic checks outside the model; her four targets are evals. She does not claim this is a principled position, and says so in the document, which is more intellectually honest than most PRDs manage.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied PRDs writes complete documents. Someone who has internalised them writes documents of visibly uneven density, and can tell you, for each dense passage, the number it is protecting. That is the single most reliable outward sign.

There are others. A master reads their own draft as an adversary before circulating it, hunting for sentences that two competent readers could resolve differently, and they can name the two readers. They know which of their claims are cheap to test and they test those before writing, rather than writing a requirement that assumes an answer a twenty-minute call would have provided. They put the argument they expect to lose in the document explicitly, because a documented objection that was considered and overruled is far more durable than an objection that was never raised. They resist the pull to make the document comprehensive, understanding that a reviewer's attention is the scarcest input and that every additional page taxes it. They can say, for any requirement, what evidence would make them delete it. And — the hardest one — they can tell when the correct PRD is no PRD: when the problem is still a guess, when the change is reversible in an afternoon, when the whole thing is one person's two-day build. Competent practitioners escalate documentation when they feel uncertain; experts notice that the feeling of uncertainty and the cost of being wrong are different quantities, and allocate to the second.

Finally, mastery shows in what happens after the document. A PRD that was written well produces a spec review where the disagreements are about the right things, an estimate that holds, and a launch where nobody is surprised. None of that is visible as achievement. The observable output of excellent requirements work is the absence of a particular class of meeting, which is why the skill is chronically under-credited and why practitioners must learn to value it on their own account.

12. What each of them decided

Aditya froze the board on 12 March 2026 with the larger cell footprint but the smaller cell fitted — a decision that cost about ₹41 per unit in unused board area and bought the option to increase capacity later without tooling. The PRD said so explicitly, in a paragraph headed "constraints we are buying options against", and stated the condition under which the option would be exercised: if field data showed more than four drift events per device per month across any distributor, the larger cell would go into the next production run. The requirements section carried the caps, the state-space classification, and twelve open questions with owners. The dashboard section ran to a page and a half and was deliberately under-specified. Of the eleven hours spent on the sampling sentence, he judged afterwards that eight had been necessary and three had been him enjoying himself.

Rhea signed the pilot on 3 March with the 8:1 cost asymmetry, the 400-case evaluation set and the twelve invariants written into an annexe that the TPA's own compliance head countersigned — a move that converted the most contested part of her PRD into a contractual artefact and, by doing so, made it the one part of the document that could not quietly drift. The 51 per cent first-month result was short of the 55 per cent threshold. Because the document had specified how the evaluation set was stratified, the shortfall was attributed within nine days to hospitals without digital discharge systems, and the remediation — a different prompting path plus a human-in-the-loop queue for that stratum — was scoped as an amendment rather than a renegotiation. The pilot was extended.

Questions for discussion.

  1. Aditya spent eleven hours on a single sentence and under-specified an entire dashboard. Was that allocation defensible, or did he simply spend his hours where he was most comfortable — on the part of the product closest to the physics? What evidence would distinguish the two explanations, and could he have gathered it beforehand?
  2. Rhea converted her invariants into a contractual annexe countersigned by the customer. This made them durable and also made them extremely expensive to change. Under what conditions is it right to move a requirement out of a document you control and into one you do not — and what did she give up?
  3. Nishtha's recovery replaced one document with five and shipped eleven weeks after restarting. A critic could argue that the original document was fine and the real failure was the absence of per-requirement owners, which is a management problem rather than a documentation one. Steelman that critic. If they are right, what does it imply about how much of PRD practice is really about writing at all?

13. Going deeper

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc
Places the PRD among its neighbours so you can tell when the answer is a different artefact entirely — which, per section 4, is often.
Writing a solution hypothesis
The upstream artefact. When the problem section cannot be written without "we believe", this is what you should be writing instead.
Goals and non-goals
The section with the highest ratio of political consequence to word count; worth studying on its own, especially the refusal/deferral/exclusion distinction.
Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N)
The narrative school's practical technique, and the best available cure for a requirements section that has lost contact with a human being.
Acceptance criteria and error cases
Link two of the traceability chain. Converts each requirement into pass/fail conditions a tester or a coding agent can check.
Telemetry requirements
Link three, the one that breaks. What must be emitted, at what grain, for any metric in your document to be computable at all.
Non-functional requirements
Latency, availability, failover, retention. In Aditya's world these are the requirements; in most PRDs they are an afterthought that surfaces as an incident.
Release criteria and success metrics
Link four. Separates "built as specified" from "safe to ship" from "worked" — three different questions teams routinely merge.
User stories and epics
The agile school's unit. Understand where it complements a PRD and where teams use it to avoid writing one.
Edge cases, states and permissions
The discipline behind the 72-cell classification in section 3; the highest-yield habit in this whole topic.
Requirements traceability
The formal machinery for the four-link chain, and mandatory reading for anyone in a regulated or audited domain.
Requirements across multiple teams
The contract-plus-local pattern that rescued Nishtha, treated properly rather than anecdotally.
Specifying APIs and data contracts
What goes in the contract PRD: interfaces, invariants, versioning and deprecation — promises to consumers you cannot poll.
Running a spec review
Where the document's claims meet their falsifiers. Given that reviewer attention is now the binding constraint, this is arguably the highest-leverage adjacent skill.
Keeping specs alive
What happens after "estimated against revision 6", and how mature teams avoid both frozen fiction and undocumented drift.
Behavioural specification for AI products
Rhea's problem, treated directly: invariants, evaluation sets, thresholds and cost asymmetries.
Specifying AI features
The practical companion — sampling, labelling, ground truth and what a distributional requirement must state.
The spec as a prompt for an AI builder
The executable-spec school's current frontier, and the direct test of whether your requirements are as unambiguous as you believe.
Hardware product requirements documents
Layering, freeze dates and derivation records — Aditya's problem, treated properly.
Product briefs for physical goods
Where tolerance bands, cost of goods and regulatory marks replace behaviours as the primary unit of requirement.
Compliance and audit requirements
What changes when a subset of your document becomes evidence rather than prose.
Writing a one-pager
The discipline of deciding what not to include; the best available training for allocating depth per claim.
Writing clearly
Underneath all of it. Most ambiguity in PRDs is not conceptual; it is sentences with two grammatical readings and nobody to notice.

Vallam Systems: Forty-One Requirements and Eighty-Eight Issues

A returns-and-claims module passed every requirement it was written against. Twelve days after it reached Dubai, the client's operations head counted eighty-eight problems. Bengaluru, Sunday, 25 October 2026.

1The night before

Gowri Mannadiar had her balcony door open in Indiranagar at half past eleven on Sunday night, 25 October 2026, with four options on the screen that she had not written. Her head of delivery had sent them from Kochi on Friday, costed in engineer-days and in weeks of contractual delay. She was to put one of them to the executive team at half past nine on Monday; Gokulan Moodithaya, who runs e-commerce operations for the Mangalath Group in Dubai, wanted a written answer by Wednesday.

What she kept returning to was one line in the quality report of 29 September: forty-one of forty-one requirements passed. The module had been built exactly as specified, had met one of the two metrics the specification named in both markets, and was now the subject of an escalation using the word unusable. The board met on Friday, 4 December, and had asked her in July for a requirements standard by the year's end.

2Vallam Systems, 2018–2026

Vallam Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Gopakumar Mayya and two classmates, to sell warehouse and returns software to Indian brands that had outgrown spreadsheets and could not afford the suites. By 30 September 2026 it had 310 employees — 104 in engineering, 7 in product, 22 implementation consultants, 177 elsewhere — and recurring revenue of ₹74.0 crore across 96 enterprise tenants: 88 in India at ₹58.6 crore, 6 in the Gulf at ₹11.4 crore, 2 elsewhere at ₹4.0 crore. That puts ₹15.4 crore, or 20.8 per cent, outside India.

The decision that shaped all of it was taken on 9 February 2021, when Vallam had 11 tenants and a median implementation of nineteen weeks. An operating note approved that month settled two things: client-specific requirements would be captured by implementation consultants in a spreadsheet called a blueprint sheet and signed by the client, not by product managers in a requirements document; and the platform would carry no client forks, only configuration. Implementation fell to a seven-week median and the tenant count rose to 96. Five years on, there is no fork in which to hide a client-specific rule.

3The industry

Indian e-commerce returns are a volume business of narrow margins. Flipkart, Amazon India, Meesho, Myntra and Nykaa run return rates that in apparel reach a quarter of orders, and reverse logistics through Delhivery, Ecom Express and Shadowfax has pushed damaged-goods inspection back into the warehouse. Software for the problem is contested — Unicommerce, Increff and EasyEcom all sell into it — and buyers now ask about configurability in the first meeting, because the last suite they bought could not be bent.

Two regulatory facts bear on the module directly. Under the GST law a credit note for a supply made in a financial year must be issued by 30 November following the end of that year, so an unadjudicated damage claim from 2025–26 becomes a permanent loss to the seller after 30 November 2026. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the inspection photographs that accompany every claim, which carry customer names and addresses; in the Gulf, the United Arab Emirates' personal data law of 2021 and Mangalath's procurement terms require that its photographs stay in a Dubai region. Indian software companies are judged by enterprise buyers, with Zoho and Freshworks as the reference points, on whether one codebase can carry both regimes.

4What happened, and what was believed at the time

Illustration 1 sets out the sequence and Exhibit 1 sets the three documents side by side. The contract with the Mangalath Group, a Kerala-founded hypermarket and online retailer headquartered in Dubai with 41 stores across the UAE and Oman, was signed on Tuesday, 14 April 2026; clause 7.2 required a Blueprint Document to be agreed within ninety days, by 13 July.

On Friday, 12 June, Geevani Mundakkal issued PRD-214 v1 after three days of workshops in Dubai. What was believed then, and recorded in the document's own summary, was that the India behaviour would carry to the Gulf with configuration. On Friday, 3 July, Girishankar Melethil and Mangalath's head of information technology signed blueprint sheet BP-77: 41 rows, of which 7 described behaviour v1 did not mention and 3 contradicted it outright. Nine rows carried the note acceptance to be agreed.

PRD-214 v3 followed on Friday, 24 July, renumbered to one requirement per blueprint row. Two of the three contradicting rows were resolved by adopting the blueprint's wording; the third became open question 4. On 29 July engineering estimated 142 engineer-days; the build ran from 3 August to 25 September over 40 working days and took 171, an overrun of 29 engineer-days or 20.4 per cent. On Tuesday, 29 September the quality report recorded 41 of 41 requirements passing, three of the six open questions still open. Release 14 reached the India tenants on 1 October and the Mangalath tenant on Thursday, 8 October.

Two days before cutover, on 6 October, Mr Moodithaya's team circulated an internal Returns Operating Note; nobody at Vallam saw it until 21 October. Exhibits 3 and 4 set out what the twelve days after cutover produced. On 22 October the analytics team in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru, produced Exhibit 2; on 23 October Mr Melethil costed the four options of Exhibit 5.

5The people

Gowri Mannadiar, head of product, Bengaluru, three years. Position: build nothing until a document the client can sign says what done means. Incentive: the board wants a requirements standard from her by December. Not saying: she approved v3 without opening BP-77, and the three questions still open at release were hers to close.

Gopakumar Mayya, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: pay whatever the delay costs and protect the February roadmap; the company did not reach 96 tenants by stopping to write. Incentive: a Series C round in early 2027 that needs the Gulf logo. Not saying: he has told two directors acceptance will land in December.

Gururaj Moolya, vice-president of engineering, Pune, five years. Position: the squad built what the document said and the quality report proves it; a tenant rules layer needs a migration across all 96 tenants. Incentive: Release 15's scope is signed. Not saying: most of the 29-engineer-day overrun went on the three unresolved open questions, which his engineers settled by picking an interpretation and recording nothing.

Geevani Mundakkal, product manager, Returns & Claims, Bengaluru, fourteen months. Position: an acceptance criterion against each requirement, written before code, would have caught this; she offered in July and was told there was no time. Incentive: promotion in January. Not saying: her June workshops were with Mangalath's IT function and she has never spoken to a store operations manager.

Girishankar Melethil, head of delivery, Kochi, six years. Position: BP-77 is the document clause 7.2 names, both sides signed it, and the module conforms. Incentive: implementation margin is measured in weeks to go-live and the blueprint model is his. Not saying: he raised the nine unagreed acceptance rows on 3 July, got nothing back, and let it go.

Garv Madhyastha, chief revenue officer, Newark, New Jersey, who wrote to Bengaluru at 08:12 on Sunday morning, 17:42 IST. Position: the 30 November date is not to be reopened; the Gulf pipeline is sold on this reference. Incentive: ₹14 crore of Gulf revenue in his 2027 quota. Not saying: he agreed the weekly credit in April to close the deal, unreviewed in India.

Glory Muthalaly, customer success lead, Gulf and Asia-Pacific, Singapore, four years. Position: the grievance is the review queue, not the document. Incentive: Mangalath's first annual review falls in April 2027 and sits in her book. Not saying: since 14 October two contractors in Kochi have cleared the client's manual queue by hand on Mangalath logins, at ₹2.6 lakh a month booked to her cost centre.

6Exhibits

7Voices

The escalation arrived at 09:40 Gulf time on Tuesday, 20 October, 11:10 in Bengaluru, to Mr Madhyastha and to nobody below him.

Eighty-eight issues in twelve days. My people in 41 stores are photographing damaged stock and the system refuses the claim because the photograph did not upload on a handset in a basement. I did not sign your PRD. I signed the blueprint, and in October my operations team wrote down how this has to work.

Gokulan Moodithaya, group head of e-commerce operations, Mangalath Group

At the post-mortem of 21 October, two readings of the evidence sat across the table.

Forty-one of forty-one requirements passed on 29 September. Nineteen of his items ask for behaviour no document we hold asks for. If conformance is not the test, tell me what is, and tell me before I sign the next release.

Gururaj Moolya, vice-president of engineering, Pune

R-29 says the system shall auto-reject a claim where the inspection photograph is missing. Open question 4, four pages later in the same document, asks whether photo-missing should auto-reject or hold for store review. Both were in v3 on 24 July. Nobody caught it, including me.

Geevani Mundakkal, product manager

Extract · BP-77, row 29, signed 3 July 2026

“Where photo not uploaded, claim to be held for store review. Store supervisor to attach photo within 48 hours.”

Not one of the four options clears the 2,612 reviews that stood open in his queue on Monday the 19th. He is not escalating a document. He is escalating a backlog his supervisors must clear before Thursday's stock count, and every week we argue about which paper governs, that number goes up.

Glory Muthalaly, Singapore, 14:05 SGT on Saturday 24 October, 11:35 IST

Gowri, I am not paying the ninety-six-lakh cap to win an argument about document structure. Bring me the option that gets his signature. If the honest answer is that we never asked his operations people anything, say that on Monday, not on 4 December.

Gopakumar Mayya, voice note, 24 October

8The options as Ms Mannadiar sees them

Option 1 — Re-specify, then build

Rewrite PRD-214 to carry non-goals, non-functional requirements, a metric set and an acceptance criterion against each of the 41 requirements; take it to Mr Moodithaya's operations team for signature; then fix the 29 defects and build the client's 8 change requests. 87 engineer-days against 78 available, ₹10.44 lakh, acceptance on 14 December on Mr Melethil's estimate. BP-77 remains the contractual document and the review queue is untouched.

Option 2 — Ship what is built

Fix the 29 defects, hold the 19 works-as-specified items outside Release 15, defer all 13 change requests to Release 16 in February 2027. 24 engineer-days and ₹2.88 lakh. Acceptance rests on the client signing against conformance to BP-77 and PRD-214 v3; four weeks withheld is ₹48.00 lakh and acceptance on 28 December.

Option 3 — Tenant configuration layer

Build a tenant-level rules layer so that photo handling, review routing and credit-note timing can differ by tenant without a fork. 94 engineer-days against 78 available, ₹11.28 lakh, and a schema migration across all 96 tenants. Mr Melethil's estimate is five weeks past 30 November, falling on 4 January 2027.

Option 4 — Acceptance criteria as the contract

Have the quality engineer write acceptance criteria covering the 41 blueprint rows and all 39 client issues, put those to the client for signature in place of any specification, and build what is signed: the 29 defects, the 5 internal change requests and 3 of the client's 8. 64 engineer-days and ₹7.68 lakh, acceptance on 7 December on the same estimate. The nine rows marked to be agreed would be settled in the process.

9The deadline and the hard constraints

Money and contract. Three years at ₹8.80 crore a year, ₹26.40 crore in all, on an implementation fee of ₹3.20 crore of which ₹1.60 crore falls due on acceptance. Credits run at ₹12 lakh per completed week past 30 November, capped at ₹96 lakh, and from 1 January 2027 Mangalath may terminate for cause if acceptance has not been achieved. Mangalath is ₹8.80 crore of Vallam's ₹74.0 crore, 11.9 per cent.

People and the window. 78 engineer-days to Friday 13 November. The freeze opens on 16 November and Mr Moolya runs regression windows fortnightly, so work missing 13 November waits for the window opening on 30 November.

Regulation. 3,180 older India claims from 2025–26, outside the Exhibit 2 windows, are still unadjudicated; their credit notes must be issued by 30 November or the sellers lose the credit, and at October's ₹412 average they carry ₹13.10 lakh. Inspection photographs fall under the DPDP Act, and Mangalath's must stay in a Dubai region.

The 2021 principle. One codebase, configuration only, no client forks — and clause 7.2 makes the Blueprint Document, not the PRD, the agreed specification.

  3. Exhibit 3 and Mr Moodithaya's email put three counts on the same twelve days: 88, 61 and 39. Which would you take to the board, and what would you say about the other two?
  4. Section 9 sets out four hard constraints. Which binds first, and would any option in Exhibit 5 change which one binds?
  5. Clause 7.2 names a document. Who at the Mangalath Group has authority to accept the module, and what, on this evidence, would they be accepting?
  6. It is 09:30 on Monday, 26 October. What should Ms Mannadiar do, in what order, and what should she say to the board on 4 December about how requirements will be written at Vallam?

At ten past midnight she read the two metrics at the end of PRD-214 v3 again: 82.0 per cent and 31 hours in India, 75.0 per cent and, across the 250 reviews closed, 94 hours in Dubai.

She opened a new document and typed a heading PRD-214 had never carried — Non-goals — then sat looking at the empty line beneath it, because the first thing she wanted to write there was the name of a person and not a feature. It was nine hours and twenty minutes until the executive review.
case20v1-req.prd:
Talipot Collect: What the Document Must Contain

A teaching case on PRD structure

1. Opening

At 4:40 pm on Thursday 22 October 2026, Eldho Lewis sat in a glass meeting room at Talipot Systems' Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, with a blank page open on his laptop and a kickoff call twenty minutes away. As Head of Product for Talipot Collect, he owned Fee Plans, a feature that would let parents pay school and coaching fees in monthly instalments through UPI AutoPay. The chief executive wanted it live before the January admissions season. Engineering would commit its capacity at sprint planning on Monday 2 November, so whatever document Eldho circulated had to exist by Friday 30 October.

The 5:00 pm IST call would join Elsamma Lazarus in Pune, Elizabeth Lopes in Berlin, where it was 1:30 pm, and Esakki Louis in New Jersey, where it was 7:30 am. The document would be the team's shared picture of Fee Plans until release. Eldho had to decide how much of it to write, and in what shape.

2. Company background

Talipot Systems was founded in Kochi in 2019 and moved to Bengaluru in 2021. Talipot Collect helps private schools, coaching institutes and music and sports academies collect fees by UPI, cards and net banking, match payments to student records and send receipts. At 30 September 2026 it served 3,400 institutions in 46 cities, with annual recurring revenue of ₹24 crore, and it had processed ₹1,150 crore of fees in the financial year to March 2026. The company employed 210 people.

Its competitors were mostly general-purpose. Razorpay and PhonePe sold payment links and pages, Paytm sold fee-payment tools, Zoho Billing handled invoices, and many schools still used their own bank's portal. Instalments collected through NPCI's UPI AutoPay, within the RBI's e-mandate rules, were something customers had asked for repeatedly and Collect did not yet offer.

3. The situation

Eldho's one-page note described a first release in which an institution defines an instalment plan, a parent authorises a UPI AutoPay mandate, Talipot debits on each due date and reconciles it, and a failed debit triggers a reminder. Elsamma had read it and sized the work at 30 engineer-weeks for her six engineers, four in Pune and two in Bengaluru. That figure excluded collection by card in other currencies.

The exclusion mattered to Esakki, who was negotiating with a Dubai group of twelve Indian-curriculum schools for a contract of ₹96 lakh a year. Its parents paid by card, in dirhams. On 14 October he had told the group that instalments were coming, and he wanted a demonstration for its procurement committee by Thursday 3 December.

The team had been here before. Exhibit 1 lists the three features released since January 2026, whose documents ranged from a one-page brief to an eleven-page specification. Elsamma remembered Late-fee Waivers: "We built waivers per student, because that is what the brief said. Institutes wanted them per class. Nobody had written down who the user was." Elizabeth remembered drawing the Waivers screens from voice notes recorded in Pune.

4. The people

Eldho Lewis, Head of Product, Bengaluru. He joined in 2021 as a product manager and was promoted to Head of Product in 2024. He owns the document and the 2 November commitment, and wants one the whole team will actually use.

Elsamma Lazarus, engineering manager, Pune, leads six engineers. She wants a scope that stays put and error cases written down, and she does not want another build that runs far past its plan.

Elizabeth Lopes, product designer, Berlin, wants to know who the user is, what a failed mandate looks like to a parent, and what consent the DPDP Act, 2023 requires for data about children, before she draws a screen. Germany's clocks fall back on 25 October, widening her gap with Bengaluru from 3.5 hours to 4.5.

Esakki Louis, sales head, New Jersey, wants dirham card collection in the first release and a working demonstration by 3 December.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows overruns of one to eight engineer-weeks, ₹7.8 lakh in all, a pooled 72.2 per cent over plan. The Parts column counts how many of the seven parts each document contained: two, three and five. Late-fee Waivers, planned at six engineer-weeks, took fourteen.

Exhibit 2 puts Elsamma's sizing beside the capacity each option leaves. Exhibit 3 draws the same dates to scale and adds the Dubai demonstration, Diwali on Sunday 8 November, and the release on Friday 18 December that the chief executive had set.

6. The options

Option A: the whole PRD first. Eldho writes all seven parts for the whole product, with requirements and error cases for every flow, and circulates nothing until it is finished. He estimates fifteen working days, which puts it in the team's hands on Wednesday 11 November and moves the start of building to Monday 16 November. Pune and Berlin would share one written reference for every flow, and Elizabeth would design against stated requirements. The release date stays 18 December; the Dubai request would be settled in writing before any engineer starts.

Option B: a brief and designs. Eldho circulates a one-page problem and solution sketch with Elizabeth's screens on Monday 26 October, three working days of effort, and engineers raise questions in daily stand-ups. Building starts on 2 November. Requirements, error cases, goals and non-goals stay unwritten unless a question prompts them, and the dirham question is left open.

Option C: a staged PRD. Eldho writes personas, problem, goals, non-goals, solution and metrics in full by Thursday 29 October. He writes requirements, acceptance criteria and error cases only for slice one, creating a plan and setting up a mandate, which Elsamma sized at 18 of the 30 engineer-weeks. Later slices, including failed-debit reminders, carry headings only until each enters build. Building starts on 2 November, and requirements for later slices are written while earlier ones are under construction.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 records the document and the outcome for three features. What may a reader conclude from it about the link between the two, and what would they need to know before concluding more?
  2. Esakki asks for dirham card collection in the first release. What would the goals and non-goals of the PRD have to say for Eldho to answer him on 30 October, and what on this page bears on that answer?
  3. Set Elsamma's sizing against the engineer-weeks each option in Exhibit 2 leaves. What further information would change your reading?
  4. Which option should Eldho take to the 2 November planning meeting, and what should he tell each of the other three people about what they will and will not find in the document?

8. A note for the learner

A PRD is a set of written answers to questions a builder would otherwise settle by guessing. Its seven parts answer different ones: for whom, what problem, to what end, what is out, what solution, in what detail, and how success will be known. The decision is therefore not between a long document and a short one. It is which questions must be answered in writing before building starts, and which can wait until a slice enters build.

A well-reasoned answer states its criterion, reads Exhibit 1 with its limits in view, prices the calendar in Exhibit 2, and treats the Dubai request as a decision to be made explicitly rather than an omission.

One defensible path is Option C, beginning with the dirham question settled on paper. The parts written in full are inexpensive and set direction: user, problem, goals, non-goals and metrics. Requirements are costly and go stale, so writing them slice by slice ties effort to what is being built. Eldho could list dirham card collection under non-goals for release one, noting the estimated nine further engineer-weeks and a date to revisit it if the group signs. The path has costs: later slices stay thin, Pune must accept requirements arriving mid-build, and Esakki hears "not in release one". A reader who weighs the ₹96 lakh contract more heavily could defend a different path; this note shows one.
