PRD Structure: What a Document Needs to Contain Before a Team Can Build the Right Thing

A product requirements document is not a formality that follows a decision. Written well, it is the decision — the place where a vague intention becomes something specific enough to be wrong, and therefore specific enough to be checked.

1. Six weeks, eighty-four alerts a day, and a renewal on the line

On the second Monday of January 2026, Kavya Menon, senior product manager at Ishira Diagnostics, a Bengaluru-based company that sells AI-assisted radiology triage software to hospital networks, sat down with a blank document and a deadline. Ishira's software reads chest X-rays and CT scans as they are uploaded, flags studies that look like they contain a critical finding — a pneumothorax, an aortic dissection, a large intracranial bleed — and routes them for faster human review. The company's largest customer, a twenty-two-hospital network across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, processed roughly 1,400 imaging studies a day through Ishira's pipeline. About six percent of those studies, some eighty-four a day, were flagged critical by the model.

The problem was what happened after the flag. Today, a flagged study landed in a shared queue that on-call teleradiologists checked between other work, nudged along by a WhatsApp group that someone had set up eighteen months earlier and nobody had since redesigned. The median time between an AI flag and a radiologist actually opening the case was three hours and forty minutes; on the worst eight percent of alerts, it ran past four hours. The hospital network's chief medical officer had made clear, in a renewal conversation Kavya had sat in on the previous week, that this was no longer acceptable: the contract, worth a meaningful share of Ishira's annual revenue, would not be renewed in its current form unless critical alerts reached a radiologist with a median time under fifteen minutes, and a 95th-percentile time under thirty. Kavya had six weeks to get a rebuilt escalation feature into production. Her first task was not to open a design tool or write a line of code. It was to write the PRD — the document that would tell two backend engineers, one mobile engineer, a designer, and a compliance reviewer exactly what "solved" meant, in language specific enough that all five of them could look at the finished feature and agree, without arguing, whether it matched what had been promised.

2. The idea

A product requirements document, PRD for short, is the artefact that translates a validated problem into instructions a build team can act on without guessing: who the feature is for, what problem it solves and does not attempt to solve, how it should behave, and how the team will know afterward whether it worked. The term and the rough shape date back to Silicon Valley hardware and software practice of the 1980s and 1990s — Marty Cagan's writing at HP and later at Silicon Valley Product Group, and Ben Horowitz's widely circulated 1995 Netscape memo "Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager," both describe the PRD as the deliverable that separates PMs who merely relay feature requests from those who define what the product actually needs to be. Before that, the same function was served by looser "market requirements documents," written for sales teams rather than engineers; the PRD's contribution was to make the document precise enough to build from, not just persuasive enough to sell.

The sentence Kavya could have repeated in the renewal meeting without sounding glib is this: a PRD is the document that turns "we need faster escalation" into a set of claims — about users, about scope, about behaviour, about success — that an engineer can build against and a skeptic can test. It is not a pitch, not a wireframe, and not a to-do list. It is closer to a contract that the product organisation writes with itself, one specific enough that six weeks later everyone can check whether it was kept.

3. How it actually works

A working PRD is built from six moving parts, and the order in which they appear is not arbitrary — each section constrains the one that follows it, which is precisely why skipping the order produces documents that read fluently but build the wrong thing.

Personas come first because every later claim is a claim about someone specific. For the alerting feature, Kavya named two: the on-call teleradiologist who receives the escalation, and the hospital's duty nurse manager who needs to see, at a glance, that a critical finding has been acknowledged. A PRD that skips personas tends to drift toward whoever is easiest to picture — usually the customer's most senior stakeholder — and quietly under-serves the person who will actually touch the feature forty times a shift.

Problem states, in the language of those personas, what is currently wrong and why it matters, with evidence rather than assertion: the 220-minute median, the four-hour tail, the CMO's ultimatum. A problem statement earns its place only if it would still be true under several different solutions — if it can only be satisfied by the one feature the author already had in mind, it is not a problem statement, it is a solution wearing a disguise.

Goals and non-goals convert the problem into a boundary. The goal was explicit — median escalation time under fifteen minutes, 95th percentile under thirty, measured from the moment the model classifies a study as critical to the moment a radiologist opens it. The non-goals were just as load-bearing: this release would not build an auto-resolution capability that closed out alerts without a human radiologist's sign-off, and it would not extend to outpatient imaging centres outside the twenty-two hospitals, however much the sales team wanted that scope added for free.

Solution is the one paragraph of the document that describes, in prose a non-engineer can follow, the shape of the fix Ishira intended to build: a tiered on-call paging system with mandatory acknowledgment and automatic re-escalation. This section deliberately stays short and readable — its job is to give a reviewer, in under a minute, enough of a mental model to evaluate whether the requirements that follow actually deliver it.

Requirements are the testable behaviours that make the solution real: what the system must do, under what conditions, with what limits, stated precisely enough that two competent engineers reading the same line would build the same thing. This is where most of the document's length and most of its arguments live, and it is the section examined in detail in the worked example below.

Metrics close the loop by naming, in advance, the numbers that will say whether the feature worked — not vague aspirations but specific measures with baselines and targets, the same figures the goals section promised, now instrumented and dated.

Exhibit A. The six sections of a PRD, read left to right as a dependency chain rather than a checklist. Skipping the order — for instance, writing Requirements before Goals & Non-Goals are settled — is the single most common structural failure Kavya sees in draft PRDs at Ishira.

4. A worked example: the escalation requirement, twice

Kavya's requirements section did not open with a feature description. It opened with the arithmetic that justified the feature, because a requirements section that cannot show its numbers is asking engineering to trust an adjective. Ishira's pipeline flags roughly eighty-four critical studies a day across the twenty-two hospitals, but that volume is not spread evenly: pulling six months of logs, Kavya found that 45 percent of daily flags land in a four-hour morning window, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., when outpatient imaging and post-operative scans cluster. That is 38 alerts in four hours, one roughly every 6.3 minutes. A radiologist doing a proper triage read — opening the study, checking the flagged region, deciding on next steps — takes about four minutes per case. A single on-call radiologist handling that peak window alone is therefore working at close to 63 percent utilisation (4 minutes of work arriving every 6.3 minutes), and single-server queues behave badly well before they hit 100 percent: waiting time rises steeply, not gently, as utilisation climbs past roughly 60–70 percent, because any case that runs long has nowhere to go but the back of a lengthening line. That queuing reality, not a vague sense that "one person isn't enough," is what forced the requirement: during the 9 a.m.–1 p.m. window, at least two radiologists must be concurrently reachable on the critical-alert pager rotation; outside that window, one on-call radiologist is sufficient. Two radiologists sharing 38 alerts brings each one's effective utilisation down to roughly 32 percent, comfortably inside the range where median wait stays close to service time rather than compounding.

The requirement did not stop at staffing. It specified the escalation mechanics precisely: the system pages the primary on-call radiologist by push notification and SMS within 90 seconds of a critical classification; if there is no acknowledgment within five minutes, it automatically pages the secondary on-call radiologist while keeping the first alert live; if there is still no acknowledgment within ten minutes, it pages the shift lead and flags the case red in the nurse manager's dashboard. Every one of those numbers — 90 seconds, five minutes, ten minutes — is a testable claim, not a description of intent, which is exactly what lets an engineer build it and a QA reviewer check it.

The second pass is where Kavya tested whether the requirement would survive success. The hospital network had already signalled it wanted to add fifteen more facilities within the year, which would push daily volume from 1,400 studies to roughly 2,300, and critical flags from 84 a day to about 138. Run the same arithmetic: 45 percent of 138 is 62 alerts in the same four-hour peak window, one every roughly 3.9 minutes. Against a four-minute service time, two radiologists would now sit at about 51 percent utilisation each — workable, but close enough to the danger zone that a single sick day or a run of complex cases could push wait times back over target. The honest requirement, stated in the PRD rather than discovered during an outage, was a staffing trigger: if daily critical-alert volume in the peak window exceeds 50, add a third concurrent on-call radiologist for that window. Changing one input — hospital count — did not just change a number on a dashboard; it changed which requirement was true, and writing that down in advance is what separated Kavya's document from a description of the system as it existed the day she wrote it.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

A PRD is not a spec

The PRD says what the escalation feature must do and why — page within ninety seconds, re-escalate within five minutes — and it stops there. It does not say which message queue carries the page, what the retry backoff looks like, or how the on-call roster is stored in the database. Those decisions belong in an engineering spec, written by the engineers, after the PRD. PMs who blur this distinction tend to fill the requirements section with implementation detail they are not qualified to defend, which does two kinds of damage: it removes the engineering team's room to find a better mechanism, and it makes the document wrong in a different, more embarrassing way — wrong about technology rather than about the customer.

Non-goal, future scope, and out of scope are three different things

A non-goal is a deliberate refusal — Ishira will not, in this feature or any near-term one, let the system resolve a critical alert without a human radiologist confirming it, because the regulatory and clinical-liability stakes make that a line the company does not intend to cross soon. Future scope is a deferral — extending the alerting system to outpatient imaging centres is plausible and even likely, just not in this six-week release. Out of scope is simply irrelevant and usually doesn't need to be written down at all — nobody was proposing that this PRD also cover billing reconciliation. Writing a non-goal as if it were a future-scope item quietly promises something the team never agreed to build.

Requirements describe behaviour, not screens

"The nurse manager dashboard should have a red banner" is a design decision. "An unacknowledged critical alert must be visually distinguishable from an acknowledged one within the nurse manager's view, in a way readable at a glance from across a nursing station" is a requirement — it is testable, and it leaves the actual visual treatment to the designer, who may have a better idea than red.

A PRD is a living document up to a point, then it should stop moving

Kavya's draft went through four real revisions in the first ten days, as the staffing arithmetic surfaced and the compliance reviewer flagged that a fully automatic third-radiologist trigger needed a human approval step to avoid unplanned overtime costs. That churn is healthy before a spec review. After the spec review, when engineering has estimated the six weeks against the document as written, the PRD should stop moving except through an explicit, logged change — otherwise "requirements" becomes a polite word for "whatever we're discussing in Slack today," and the estimate attached to it becomes fiction.

Depth should track how reversible and how risky the decision is

A copy change to a button is a decision you can undo in an afternoon and barely deserves a one-pager. An alerting system that pages a radiologist about a possible aortic dissection is close to irreversible in its consequences if it fails quietly, and it sits inside a regulated clinical workflow — that is exactly the kind of decision that earns a fully worked PRD with staffing arithmetic and a compliance sign-off line, not because process is virtuous in itself but because the cost of being wrong is not symmetric.

Metrics need a floor as well as a target

The success metric was escalation time. The guardrail metric, added after a candid conversation with the on-call radiologists themselves, was alert-fatigue rate — the share of pages that turned out, on review, to be false positives serious enough that a radiologist felt paged unnecessarily. A PRD optimised purely for speed could hit its fifteen-minute target by paging radiologists on every borderline finding, and burn out the very staff the feature depended on within a month. A target without a guardrail is an invitation to game the target.

Different readers use the document for different purposes

Engineering reads the requirements section for what to estimate. Design reads personas and solution for what to sketch. Legal and the clinical-compliance reviewer, in Ishira's case, reads goals and non-goals almost exclusively, because that section is where liability boundaries live — and in a health-technology company operating under India's evolving software-as-a-medical-device guidance from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, an ambiguous non-goal is not a documentation nicety, it is a real exposure. A PRD that serves only one of these audiences well has not really done its job.

What a PRD cannot do

It cannot tell you that the underlying problem was real — that work belongs to discovery and research, done before the PRD exists, not inside it. It cannot guarantee good engineering execution; a precise requirement can still be built badly. And it cannot substitute for the conversations that get five stakeholders with different incentives to actually agree — a PRD documents alignment, in Kavya's experience it rarely creates it by itself. She still had to sit in the same room as the compliance reviewer and the on-call radiologists before the document reflected reality rather than her own best guess at it.

6. How the shape changes with the product and the stage

In a consumer product, personas are often broader and more inferred — "a price-sensitive weekend shopper" rather than a named clinical role — and the requirements section leans harder on measurable behaviour at scale, because you cannot interview every user the way Kavya could interview twelve teleradiologists. In a B2B product like Ishira's, personas are usually fewer, more specific, and interviewable directly, and the goals and non-goals section carries more legal and contractual weight, because a single enterprise customer's renewal can depend on a single line in that section, as it did here. In a marketplace product, the PRD structure has to do something the others don't: state requirements for at least two personas whose interests can conflict — a delivery-marketplace PRD, for instance, has to specify not just what the customer sees but what the independent rider sees, and a non-goal for one side ("we will not auto-reduce rider payouts based on this feature") is often the section that prevents a well-intentioned change from triggering a supply-side revolt.

Stage changes the document's weight more than its skeleton. At an early-stage company, a PRD is often three pages, written by the PM who will also design the interim mockups, reviewed by two people over one call, because the cost of being wrong is a wasted sprint. At a company Ishira's size, with a live clinical workflow and a compliance function, the same six sections stretch to twelve or fifteen pages, pass through a formal spec review, and carry a named sign-off line for legal — not because bigger companies love paperwork, but because the blast radius of an ambiguous requirement is a hospital-network contract rather than a sprint.

7. Common mistakes

Solutioning inside the problem statement. The symptom is a problem section that already names the feature — "we need a tiered on-call paging system" appearing on page one, before any goal has been stated. The underlying error is mistaking the thing you want to build for the thing that's wrong; the cheapest diagnostic is to ask whether the same problem sentence could justify two or three genuinely different solutions. If it can only justify the one the author already had in mind, it was never really a problem statement.

Non-goals left as an afterthought or omitted entirely. The symptom shows up three weeks into the build, when an engineer asks "wait, are we doing outpatient centres too?" and nobody can point to a sentence that says no. The underlying error is believing that stating goals implicitly rules everything else out; it doesn't, because ambition is contagious mid-project. The cheapest diagnostic is simply counting: a PRD with one non-goal sentence or none at all has not actually done this work.

Requirements without acceptance criteria. The symptom is two engineers building the same requirement two different ways and both being technically right — one interprets "escalate quickly" as ninety seconds, the other as five minutes, and QA has no document to adjudicate the dispute. The underlying error is writing a requirement as an adjective rather than a testable claim. The cheapest diagnostic, the one Kavya used on her own draft, is to read each requirement line and ask: could two competent engineers build genuinely different things and both honestly claim they met this line? If yes, the line needs a number.

Metrics defined after launch. The symptom is a team, six weeks after shipping, unable to say with confidence whether the feature worked, because nobody captured a clean baseline before the change went live and the dashboard was assembled retroactively from noisy data. The underlying error is treating metrics as a reporting exercise rather than a design input that belongs in the document before a line of code is written. The cheapest diagnostic is a single question asked at PRD-drafting time, not at launch: what number will change, and do we already have today's clean baseline for it? For Ishira, that baseline — 220 minutes, measured from six months of logs before Kavya wrote a word of the requirements section — is what made the fifteen-minute target falsifiable rather than aspirational.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks later, the escalation feature shipped on time, and the hospital network's own instrumentation showed a median escalation time of twelve minutes in its first full month, with the 95th percentile at twenty-six — inside target, though closer to the edge than Kavya was entirely comfortable with, which is its own kind of useful information for the next revision. What made the launch unremarkable, in the best sense, was that nothing in the requirements section surprised anyone by the time engineering finished building it: the compliance reviewer had signed off on the non-goals in week one, not week five; the on-call radiologists had seen the staffing numbers before the schedule changed under them; and when a mid-build question came up about whether a false-positive suppression rule counted as "auto-resolution" under the non-goal, the PRD had language specific enough to answer it in a five-minute Slack thread rather than a re-opened meeting. Good PRD work is largely invisible in exactly this way — it shows up as arguments that don't happen, not as praise that does.

9. What Kavya decided, and what to learn next

Kavya's finished PRD ran to eleven pages, structured through the six sections in order, anchored by the two exhibits reproduced above, with the staffing trigger for the hospital network's planned expansion written in before anyone asked for it. She decided, deliberately, that the requirements section would be the longest part of the document and the solution section the shortest — a ratio she'd come to trust after watching thinner requirements sections turn into disputes and thicker solution sections turn into premature design debates that had nothing to do with what the customer actually needed. The renewal was signed in the fourth week of the build, before the feature had even shipped, because the CMO's team could read the PRD's goals and non-goals section and see, in writing, exactly what they were being promised and exactly what they were not.

The natural next things to learn sit just past where this document ends. Acceptance criteria and error cases go one level deeper than the requirements section sketched here, turning each requirement into the specific pass/fail conditions a QA engineer or an AI coding agent can check line by line. Telemetry requirements ask a harder question the metrics section only gestures at: what, precisely, has to be logged, at what grain, for the fifteen-minute claim to be measurable at all rather than merely believed. And for a regulated, safety-relevant feature like this one, non-functional requirements — around latency floors, failover behaviour if the paging service itself goes down, and audit-trail retention — deserve a document of their own, because a PRD that tries to carry clinical-safety engineering inside its requirements section usually ends up doing neither job well.

Two questions are worth sitting with before writing the next one. First: for every requirement in your own draft, could two competent engineers read the same line, build genuinely different things, and both honestly claim they'd met it — and if so, what number is missing? Second: what number, unmeasured today, are you about to promise to move — and do you actually have a clean baseline for it, or only a confident guess?
